reasoning: Everyday blessing said to a man, e.g. after work. ق in يقوّي is a glottal stop and the shadda doubles w. The first vowel after y could also be e (ye'awwiik), so I am only medium on vowel quality.
Everyday verb, so ق is a glottal stop, written '. Also means pulled out or uprooted, but 'took off clothes/shoes' is a main use.
ق in 'ahwe is a glottal stop. Taa marbuta after ي is e, with yy doubled: 3arabiyye. The same coffee is also called 'ahwe saada, but this phrase is fine.
Word of MSA origin that is used in everyday speech. Urban speakers usually glottalise ق even in such words, giving ta'liidi. A more careful speaker might say taqliidi.
Word-initial hamza is a vowel seat, so it is written as just the vowel i. Alif maqsura is a. Standard Palestinian past tense, he-form.
Form VII-type passive with it- prefix (also heard as inlagha). غ is gh and final ى is a. Common in everyday speech for cancelled events.
Word-initial ق is a glottal stop and is written, so 'iTaar. ط is emphatic T and the vowel after it is long. Trains are rare locally, but the word is used normally.
ث is said t. The teen number contracts to tlaTTa3sh with emphatic doubled TT, as the spelling with ط suggests. Palestinian teen forms like khamsTa3sh work the same way.
MSA-origin political term that Palestinians use in conversation. Long uu is kept, yy is doubled, and taa marbuta after ي is e.
Religious term with no ق. ف is f and ط is emphatic T. Some speakers insert a vowel (fiTer), but the plain fiTr is standard.
Medial hamza is a glottal stop, written '. Past tense, he-form.
English loanword with a long oo. Used in the singular for the garment.
Everyday verb, so ق is a glottal stop. The vowel pattern is zihi' (he got bored). The participle is zahqaan.
Urban Palestinian monophthongises ay to ee, as in beet. Taa marbuta after م is e. Some speakers keep khayme.
ma3lesh is widely used in Palestine, though many say ma3leesh. ma fii means 'there isn't', and the ellipsis is not romanized. A speaker might also say ma 3indna for 'we don't have'.
Feminine imperative saami7ii plus -ni gives saami7iini, with the ح written 7.
Palestinian demonstrative for a distant feminine thing, 'that one over there'. The masculine is hadaak.
MSA-origin word used in conversation. ظ is written TH per the scheme, though some urban speakers say D or a z-like sound. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
Used for thin objects such as a pen or a slice. ع is 3 and the vowel is a long ii.
Feminine participle of ta'akkad with the colloquial mit- prefix and a medial hamza (glottal stop). Taa marbuta after د is e. Fast speech often drops the i (mit'akkde).
ل assimilates before س. ثنتين is said tinteen, with ث as t and the dual ending as ee.

il- assimilates to the emphatic ط. Tayyaara is the everyday Palestinian word for plane. The feminine participle has a hamza and a doubled kh; taa marbuta after ر is a. Fast speech may reduce it to mit'akhkhra.
Participle of the colloquial verb naDDaf (to clean), where Palestinians usually say D for ظ. I am unsure whether a shop would say munaDDif or munaTHTHif, so confidence is low.
ق in the everyday verb is a glottal stop, and ط is emphatic T. The final ة in kahraba is pronounced a, dropping the written taa marbuta. raa7at il-kahraba is a common alternative.
English loanword with a long ii and a final nz cluster. It is the normal word for jeans.
